title: What is proxy betting, and why is Bill Simmons under investigation for it?
content:
Sports personality Bill Simmons is facing scrutiny from the Massachusetts Gaming Commission after admitting on his podcast Sunday that he used his daughter’s boyfriend to place bets for him on FanDuel.

Simmons lives in California, where sports gambling is illegal. The boyfriend accessed Simmons’ account to place bets in Massachusetts.

“I get the code to make sure it’s me to my phone; I give him the code, he logs in. And I have all this money that I had from last year because I actually hit a bunch of futures last year. And he’s putting in bets for me,” Simmons, the CEO and founder of The Ringer media network, said in an episode released Sunday.

In an episode of “The Bill Simmons Podcast” released Tuesday, Simmons addressed the issue and said FanDuel, which is a sponsor of the show, voided the bets.

“I talked about how I got my daughter’s boyfriend to place some bets for me in Massachusetts, because I was in L.A.,” Simmons said. “Did not know about the proxy rules. … I learned my lesson. Apparently, proxy betting, not allowed. I actually thought it was, but that’s fine.”

Proxy betting is having another person place a sports wager on your behalf, or letting someone log into your online account and place bets. It is illegal in Massachusetts and banned by sportsbooks such as FanDuel and DraftKings for identification purposes, to prevent money laundering and to comply with state-specific regulations.

Proxy betting has also been used in cases of underage individuals bypassing age restrictions to place bets through older users’ accounts. Simmons said his daughter’s boyfriend is 21, above the legal gambling age of 18 in Massachusetts.

A FanDuel spokesperson told The Athletic they became aware of the issue and handled it “consistent with our Terms and Conditions and Massachusetts Gaming Commission regulations, including reporting the matter to the MGC.” The Massachusetts Gaming Commission said it is “aware” of the matter and “currently reviewing” it.

FanDuel’s terms and conditions state that a user could have their account permanently suspended and their winnings rescinded if they are found guilty of proxy betting.

“This includes sharing accounts among friends or family and/or having another person log into your account for purposes of placing a wager on your behalf,” the terms read.

Proxy betting has been involved in sports gambling controversies in recent years, such as the NBA’s recent scandal involving Jontay Porter in 2024. The former Toronto Raptors center was banned by the league for betting on Raptors games and manipulating his play to win wagers. The league also found that Porter placed at least 13 bets on NBA games using an associate’s online betting account.

Cleveland Guardians pitchers Emmanuel Clase and Luiz Ortiz arranged bets with co-conspirators who were in position to wager on their pitches, according to prosecutors, allowing individuals to win guaranteed prop bets. Prosecutors allege bettors used intermediaries to place the wagers based on information from the players.

FanDuel has already voided bets that Simmons placed, and any potential earnings would be forfeited. He could also face penalties from the Massachusetts Gaming Commission, which can place Simmons on a prohibited bettor’s list, legally barring him from accessing any licensed online sportsbooks or casinos in Massachusetts.

In California, proxy betting and unauthorized gambling are treated as minor infractions if the wagers do not exceed $2,500, and a first-time violation can be punished with a fine up to $250. If the wagers exceed $2,500, it can be charged as a misdemeanor and carry a sentence of up to one year in jail and substantial fines.

Simmons rose to prominence in the 1990s with his column “Sports Guy” and a Boston-focused website under a similar nickname. His success landed him at ESPN, first as a guest columnist and later as a writer on Page 2, where his popularity spread nationwide.

He later served as the editor-in-chief of Grantland, a sports and pop-culture site owned by ESPN, before leaving the company in 2015 for HBO. Simmons launched The Ringer in 2016, where he is CEO, and announced in 2020 that Spotify purchased the company for approximately $200 million.

“The Bill Simmons Podcast” ranks as the most popular sports show on Apple. Spotify describes the show as “the most downloaded sports podcast of all time.”
